readall_conflicts: The one listed work (MacKenzie et al. 2012) is silent as far as its abstract goes and its PDF could not be downloaded, so it neither supports nor contradicts the catalog. However, an on-disk source in the same our files, not in the 'works' list, downloaded by an earlier reading, bears directly on the catalog record: Thurston, William R. 1976. The Phonology of Anêm, a Non-Austronesian Language of West New Britain. MA thesis, McMaster University (file, text layer in the beside it). Its section 2.3 'Stress', thesis pp. 10-11 (PDF pages 21-22), says verbatim: "Three degrees of stress are recognized in Anem: primary /'/, secondary /,/, and non-stress, the latter unmarked in the transcription. Secondary stress is apparent only in long utterances, where one or more of several stressed vowels is more prominent that the others. Words spoken in isolation seem to have a characteristic accentuation which is not predictable: [examples 'water', 'ash', 'Mt. Andewa', 'jungle', 'bigmen'] Stress does not appear to differentiate lexical items, however. The accentuation of words in isolation often differs from their accentuation when they occur with affixes or in a sentence: [..] Probably, accentuation is morphological or syntactic; more research is required. Stress is indicated here only in citing specific utterances; forms transcribed without stress have been elicited at different times with different accentuation." audit.recode_to: fixed-dominant (penultimate), not in the strict set, with a caution: 'stress not fully analysed; penult is a tendency on isolated words; shifts under affixation/in phrases (Thurston 1976:10-11, 1982:92); not lexically contrastive'. 'undetermined' is the defensible alternative if the catalog requires a stated rule.

audit.reasoning: Quote check passes: the Thurston 1982:92 passage is verbatim in the. But the classification 'fixed-strict' (exceptionless penult, penultimate stress) is stronger than any source supports. The deciding source itself hedges ('remains to be fully analysed', 'tends to occur most frequently in penultimate position', stress 'moved.. by other morphemes', ádo ~ adó). The sole dedicated phonology, Thurston 1976 (downloaded now from MacSphere), states isolation-word accentuation 'is not predictable', lists non-penult isolation forms (/goxúp/ 'ash' final, /ándeua/ initial) alongside penult ones, says stress is not lexically distinctive, and concludes 'Probably, accentuation is morphological or syntactic; more research is required.'
